groups.title: Rural–urban migration
groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer discusses rural to urban migration.

transcript.text: Good morning. This week we're looking at one of the most important demographic changes of our time: the movement of people from rural areas to cities. I'll cover causes, consequences and some policy responses.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's population lived in cities. Today the figure is about fifty-six percent, and it continues to rise steadily.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Of course, this figure hides large regional differences. In parts of Europe and North America, more than eighty percent of people already live in cities, while in some African and Asian countries the majority are still in rural areas, and urbanisation is only beginning.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Researchers use the terms 'push' and 'pull' factors. Push factors drive people away from the countryside, such as drought or lack of jobs in farming, where mechanisation has reduced the need for labour.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Pull factors attract them to cities: higher wages, better schools and access to healthcare. In many countries, wages in cities are twice as high as in rural areas, which is a powerful incentive.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: It is rarely a single factor that decides. Most migrants weigh a combination of reasons, and many also rely on family or friends who have moved before them, which is sometimes called a network effect, helping new arrivals to find accommodation and work.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Migration has benefits for the migrants themselves, but also for those left behind. Workers send money home, known as remittances, and for some countries these payments exceed foreign aid.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: However, rapid urban growth creates problems. The most visible is informal housing, sometimes called slums, where around one billion people currently live.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Cities also offer anonymity and freedom. Young people, and women in particular, often report that city life gives them opportunities that traditional communities do not, such as choosing a career or a partner for themselves.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: In these areas, clean water and sanitation are often missing, which leads to the spread of disease. Governments face a dilemma: improving these areas may attract even more migrants.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Some governments have tried to restrict movement. China's household registration system, known as hukou, limits access to public services for people who move without permission. Critics say this creates a divided society.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: The consequences are not only about housing and services. Cities that grow too quickly can also face serious traffic problems and air pollution, which affect everyone who lives there, rich or poor.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Other countries take a different approach, investing in medium-sized towns so that people don't have to move to the capital. This reduces pressure on the largest cities and spreads economic opportunity.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: Looking ahead, climate change may become the leading push factor. The World Bank has estimated that by twenty fifty, over two hundred million people could be forced to move within their own countries.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: These estimates are uncertain, because they depend on how quickly the climate changes and how well countries adapt. Nevertheless, planners are already starting to take them seriously.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO

transcript.text: I'd like you to think about whether cities are ready for that. We'll return to the question in the seminar. Thank you.
transcript.speaker: DR OKONKWO
